---
title: "CSS by doing: layout with Flexbox and Grid"
---

Your pages so far have been a stack. One element under the other, in the order
they stand in `index.html`, because that is what the browser does when nobody
tells it otherwise. A chessboard needs eight columns. A row of weather cards
needs to sit in a line and wrap when the window gets narrow. This chapter
gives you the two tools that put boxes where you want them.

## Eight boxes that snap into a row {#sec-layout-experiment}

Create a new app from our template. In `index.html`,
replace the `<h1>` with eight empty boxes:

```html
<div id="board">
  <div class="cell"></div>
  <div class="cell"></div>
  <div class="cell"></div>
  <div class="cell"></div>
  <div class="cell"></div>
  <div class="cell"></div>
  <div class="cell"></div>
  <div class="cell"></div>
</div>
```

Replace everything in `src/index.ts` with one line:

```ts
import './styles.css';
```

Create `src/styles.css` next to it:

```css
.cell {
  height: 3rem;
  background-color: #b58863;
}
```

Run `npm start`. You get eight brown bars, each as wide as the window, stacked
from top to bottom. Now add one rule above the `.cell` rule:

```css
#board {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(8, 1fr);
  gap: 2px;
}
```

Save the file. The eight bars snap into a single row of eight boxes with a
thin line between them. Change the `8` inside `repeat(8, 1fr)` to a `4` and
save again: two rows of four. You never touched the HTML. The boxes are the
same eight `div`s in the same order, and one rule on their parent decided how
they are arranged.

## Every element is a box {#sec-layout-box}

Every element the browser draws is a rectangle, even when you never see its
edges. That rectangle has four layers, and CSS lets you set each of them.

![The four layers of an element's box. Content in the middle, then padding,
then the border, then the margin.](images/box-model.svg){width=340}

The content is the text or the image itself. Padding is space inside the
element, between the content and the border, and it is painted in the
element's background color. The border is a line you can draw around the
padding. Margin is space outside the element, between this box and its
neighbors, and it always stays transparent.

One detail catches everybody once. By default, `width` sets the width of the
*content* only, and padding and border are added on top of it. A box with
`width: 200px`, `padding: 10px`, and a 2 pixel border therefore covers 224
pixels of screen, not 200.

A `div`, a `p`, and an `h1` are **block** boxes: each takes all the width it
can get and starts on a new line. A `span` and an `a` are **inline**: they sit
inside the running text and are only as wide as their content. That is why the
eight `div`s of the experiment started life as a stack of full-width bars.

## Flexbox lays out a line {#sec-layout-flexbox}

`display: flex` on a container puts its children next to each other in one
line, and they stop taking the full width. `flex-direction: column` stands
that line upright. `gap` sets the space between the children, and
`flex-wrap: wrap` lets a child move down to a new line when the row runs out
of room.

```css
#toolbar {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: row;
  gap: 0.5rem;
}
```

Two more properties, `justify-content` and `align-items`, decide where the
children sit in the space that is left over. Their values are the research
task below.

Flexbox has many more properties than this chapter needs. When you want one,
read [MDN's basic concepts of
flexbox](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_flexible_box_layout/Basic_concepts_of_flexbox).

## Grid lays out a board {#sec-layout-grid}

Flexbox thinks in one line. A chessboard and a photo gallery are
two-dimensional, and that is Grid's job. `display: grid` together with
`grid-template-columns` says how many columns there are and how wide each one
is. The browser then fills the columns from left to right and starts a new row
whenever they are full, so you never write the rows yourself.
`repeat(8, 1fr)` is short for writing `1fr` eight times.

`gap` works in a grid too. `aspect-ratio: 1` on the children keeps every cell
exactly as tall as it is wide, no matter how wide the board gets.

[MDN's guide to CSS grid
layout](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_grid_layout) is
the place to go when a grid needs more than equal columns.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Look at the box in DevTools

Open the browser DevTools with F12, pick an element in the Elements panel, and
scroll the styles panel to the bottom. The colored box model diagram there
shows the real content, padding, border, and margin of that element in pixels.
When a layout does something you did not expect, look there first.
:::

## Sizes, colors, and type {#sec-layout-values}

Three units cover almost everything you will write this year. `px` is one
screen pixel, right for a border or a small gap. `rem` is the browser's base
font size, usually 16 pixels, so a length in `rem` grows when the reader turns
their font size up. `%` is a share of the parent element.

Colors come in three notations, and you will meet all of them in other
people's code: a name like `tomato`, a hex code like `#b58863` with two hex
digits each for red, green, and blue, and `rgb(181 136 99)` with the three
numbers spelled out.

`font-family` takes a list, and the browser uses the first font it actually
has. `font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;` asks for the operating system's own
interface font and falls back to any sans-serif font. `font-size` takes a
length, and `rem` is the safe unit for it.

Three more properties earn their place in the exercises below.
`border-radius` rounds the corners of a box, `box-shadow` paints a shadow
behind it, and `transition` makes a change happen over time instead of
instantly:

```css
.card {
  transition: transform 0.15s;
}
```

That line says: whenever this element's `transform` changes, animate the
change over 0.15 seconds. MDN documents what each of the three accepts; look
them up when you want a different corner, shadow, or speed.

::: {.research title="Centering, `1fr`, and the hover lift"}
The weather dashboard below centers the text inside every card and lifts a
card when the mouse touches it. Both need CSS that this chapter names and does
not explain.

1. With Flexbox, which two properties center a single child horizontally
   *and* vertically inside its parent, and which value does each one need?
2. In `grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr)`, what does `1fr` mean?
3. What does `justify-content: space-between` do to the children of a flex
   row?
4. What does `transform: translateY(-4px)` do to an element?

Centering with Flexbox comes back in almost every exercise from here on, so
that one has to work in the exam without looking it up.
:::

## Exercise: a chessboard {#sec-layout-chessboard}

{{< exercise chessboard >}}

The `index.html` you copied holds a `<div id="board">` with 64 `<div>`s inside
it. Every one of them has the class `cell`, plus a second class, `light` or
`dark`, that already alternates the way a real board does.

1. Replace everything in `src/index.ts` with `import './styles.css';` and run
   `npm start`. You see the heading and nothing else, because the cells are
   empty and have no height yet.
2. In `src/styles.css`, give `.cell` a height of `3rem`, give `.cell.light`
   the background color `#f0d9b5`, and give `.cell.dark` the background color
   `#b58863`. The page fills with 64 wide stripes in alternating colors.
3. Turn `#board` into a grid with eight equal columns. The stripes become an
   8 by 8 board that spans the whole window.
4. Give `#board` a width of `30rem` and center it in the window with
   `margin: 0 auto`. The board shrinks and moves to the middle of the page.
5. The cells are wide rectangles now: each column is an eighth of `30rem`,
   but the height is still stuck at `3rem`. Replace that height with
   `aspect-ratio: 1`, and every cell becomes exactly as tall as it is wide,
   whatever width you give the board.
6. Draw a frame around the board: a 4 pixel solid border on `#board`, in a
   dark brown such as `#4a3728`.
7. Now TypeScript. In `src/index.ts`, below the import, select every cell with
   `document.querySelectorAll<HTMLDivElement>('#board .cell')` and loop over
   the result with `for...of`. Give each cell a listener for the `click`
   event.
8. Inside the listener, remove the class `selected` from every cell first,
   then add it to the cell that was clicked. `src/styles.css` already carries
   a `.cell.selected` rule, so the clicked square gets a yellow ring. Click
   around the board: exactly one square is ever selected.
9. Clicking the selected square a second time should clear the selection.
   `classList.contains` tells you whether the cell was already selected,
   before your loop wipes the board.

## Exercise: a weather dashboard {#sec-layout-weather}

{{< exercise weather-dashboard >}}

The `index.html` you copied holds a `<div id="cards">` with six city cards.
Each card is a `<div>` with the class `card` and one condition class:
`sunny`, `rainy`, `cloudy`, or `snowy`. Inside a card sit an `<h2>` with the
city name, a `<p class="temperature">`, and a `<p class="condition">`.

1. Replace everything in `src/index.ts` with `import './styles.css';` and run
   `npm start`. The six cards stand under each other, one per line, with no
   card look yet.
2. Make `#cards` a flex row with a gap of `1rem`, and let the row wrap so the
   cards drop to a second line when the window gets narrow. Try it: drag the
   window edge and watch a card move down.
3. Give `.card` a width of about `11rem`, `1rem` of padding, rounded corners
   with `border-radius`, and a soft `box-shadow`.
4. Center the content of a card horizontally and vertically. Make the card
   itself a flex container with `flex-direction: column`, then use the two
   properties from the research task.
5. Write one rule per condition class that sets a `background-color` and a
   text `color` you can read on it. Pick colors that fit the weather: warm for
   `.sunny`, blue for `.rainy`, gray for `.cloudy`, pale blue for `.snowy`.
   All six cards change with four rules, because two cities share a condition.
6. Lift a card when the mouse is over it. Write a `.card:hover` rule that
   moves the card up by 4 pixels with the `transform` property from the
   research task, and add `transition: transform 0.15s;` to `.card` so the
   move is animated instead of instant.

### Optional: cycle the conditions {#sec-layout-weather-cycle}

The page carries a button with the id `nextConditionButton`. Make it move
every card one step through the four conditions: sunny to rainy, rainy to
cloudy, cloudy to snowy, and snowy back to sunny.

1. In `src/index.ts`, write an array with the four conditions in that order.
   Each entry needs two pieces, the class name and the text for the card, for
   example `{ className: 'sunny', label: 'Sunny' }`.
2. Select the button with `document.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>` and
   throw an error when it is not there. Add a `click` listener to it.
3. In the listener, select every card with
   `document.querySelectorAll<HTMLDivElement>('.card')` and loop over them.
4. For one card, find out which of the four class names it carries right now
   with `classList.contains`. Add 1 to that position, use `%` so the last
   condition wraps around to the first, remove all four class names from the
   card, and add the new one.
5. Set the text as well. `card.querySelector<HTMLParagraphElement>('.condition')`
   finds the condition paragraph inside that one card, and its `textContent`
   gets the new label.

Every click now moves all six cards one step, colors and text together.
